title: A Disconnected Superconducting Regime at the Parent Limit of Infinite-Layer Nickelates
authors: Chihao Li, Yutong Chen, Yaolong Bian, Yihao Zhang, Jiahao Ye, Zhitong An, Xingtian Sun, Yu Fan, Zhihui Chen, Zhanze Wang, Jinglei Zhang, Haichao Xu, Rui Peng, Donglai Feng
abstract: Infinite-layer nickelates have been widely viewed as cuprate analogs in which superconductivity emerges and forms a superconducting dome centered around 10-20% cation substitution. Here we show that pristine and stoichiometric PrNiO2, without cation substitution, exhibits intrinsic superconductivity characterized by zero resistance and diamagnetism in uncapped films. Through heterostructure engineering, we further exclude an interfacial origin of the superconductivity. Remarkably, zero-resistance superconductivity is consistently observed in trivalent-substituted PrNiO2, whereas it is rapidly suppressed by dilute divalent substitution. Combined with angle-resolved photoemission studies, these results indicate that such a new superconducting regime is confined to within 3% additional hole doping from pristine PrNiO2. Furthermore, this phase is separated from the previously established superconducting dome around ~ 20% divalent doping by a non-superconducting region in the phase diagram, and is further distinguished by a remarkably stronger upper-critical-field anisotropy. These findings establish a unique separated superconducting regime, suggesting that infinite-layer nickelates are not merely cuprate analogs but host distinct superconducting physics.
summary: This paper investigates superconducting behavior in infinite-layer nickelates, finding intrinsic zero-resistance superconductivity even in pristine films. Crucially, they demonstrate that this parent-state superconductivity forms a distinct regime, separated from the conventionally understood doping dome, suggesting unique electronic correlations at play.
main_problem: To determine if superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates is governed by a cuprate-like single doping dome or if an intrinsic superconducting regime exists near the parent, undoped limit.
main_result: The study establishes a unique, separated superconducting regime near the parent state, distinct from the conventional high-doping dome. This suggests that infinite-layer nickelates host distinct superconducting physics compared to cuprate analogs.
method: A combination of transport measurements (zero resistance, diamagnetism), heterostructure engineering to rule out interface effects, and Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) were employed.
model_or_system: The physical system is infinite-layer nickelates ($	ext{RENiO}_2$), studied in pristine and stoichiometric forms, with doping controlled via both isovalent ($	ext{La}/	ext{Pr}$) and aliovalent substitutions ($	ext{Sr}/	ext{Ca}$).
key_observables: Zero resistance, diamagnetism (TDO), upper-critical-field anisotropy ($\gamma$), and electronic band structure features observed via ARPES.
important_parameters: The superconducting phase is confined to a narrow doping range near the parent state ($p \approx 0.09$ holes), separated from the dome established by higher divalent doping levels.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption challenged is that all superconductivity in these materials must follow the simple, continuous doping evolution observed in cuprates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate zero resistance in uncapped films and heterostructures, confirm robustness under La substitution, show ARPES spectra comparing superconducting to lightly doped states, and map out a phase diagram showing two distinct superconducting regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the intrinsic superconductivity of pristine $	ext{PrNiO}_2$, then ruling out interfacial origins via heterostructures, mapping the doping dependence using ARPES and transport measurements, and finally contrasting this narrow parent-state regime with the established high-doping dome.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses complex many-body physics in strongly correlated oxides, providing crucial experimental constraints on theories of unconventional superconductivity that are relevant to quantum materials research.
